# On the Things We Carry in Silence

There is a particular quality of light that exists only in the first few minutes after waking, before the world has fully assembled itself. In those moments, you are not yet a person with obligations. You are not yet someone who owes anyone an explanation or a phone call or a better version of yourself. You are just a body in a room, and the light is arriving through the window the way it always does, indifferent to your particular smallness. I think about that light often. Not because it is extraordinary, but because it is one of the few moments when we are permitted to simply exist without performing existence.

We perform constantly. We perform competence at work. We perform interest in conversations that do not move us. We perform the architecture of a self — building it in real time, brick by brick, for an audience that may or may not be watching. And somewhere beneath all that scaffolding, there is a person who simply wants to sit in the kitchen and listen to the refrigerator hum. There is someone who wants to say, "I don't know what I'm doing," and not have that sentence collapse the entire fragile structure of who we have decided to be.



I don't think we talk about silence enough. Not the absence of sound — that is easy enough to describe — but silence as a space that exists between people, between words, between the things we know and the things we allow ourselves to say. Most of my life, I think, has been lived in that silence. And I suspect the same is true of almost everyone, though we would rarely admit it in a room full of other people.

Consider: when was the last time someone asked you how you are and you told the truth? Not the polished, socially acceptable truth, not the version trimmed for time or context, but the raw and unedited truth — the one that includes the thing you are actually afraid of, the grief you haven't processed, the strange and unexplainable joy that flickers through your chest for reasons you can't name. We don't do that. We say "fine" or "good" or "hanging in there," and these phrases are so worn from use that they have become almost meaningless, like coins that have been through too many pockets.

But what would happen if we answered honestly? If, one morning at the coffee machine or the school drop-off or the checkout line at the grocery store, we said, "Actually, I'm terrified"? I don't think the world would end. I think, for a moment, it might actually become more real.

## The Geography of Loneliness

Loneliness is not the same as being alone. I have been alone in mountains and felt entirely at peace, and I have been surrounded by people at a dinner table and felt the kind of isolation that makes your chest feel like it is closing. The difference, I think, is connection — not proximity, but connection. You can stand six inches from another human being and be further from them than you have ever been from anyone.

We live in an age that claims to be more connected than ever before. We have devices in our pockets that can reach almost any person on the planet. We have networks and feeds and threads and forums. We have the ability to share every passing thought, every meal, every sunset, every half-formed idea. And yet. And yet loneliness has become something like a public health crisis. People are lonelier now than they have been in decades. Perhaps it is because sharing is not the same as being known. Broadcasting yourself is not the same as being understood. You can send a thousand signals and still never be received.



I think about the difference between communication and communion. Communication is the exchange of information. It is useful, necessary, and largely mechanical. Communion is something else entirely. It is the experience of being in the presence of another person and feeling, for a moment, that the distance between your inner world and theirs has briefly collapsed. It is a recognition. It is the feeling of being seen in a way that does not require explanation.

We cannot manufacture communion. That is part of what makes it so precious and so frustrating. It happens in spite of our efforts, not because of them. It happens in the spaces we do not plan. A conversation that begins with a comment about the weather and ends with two strangers crying in a parking lot. A letter from a friend that arrives at exactly the right moment. The silence between two people who have known each other long enough that silence has become its own language.

I think the best relationships I have ever known were built not on the things people said to each other, but on the things they didn't need to say. There is a kind of knowing that is deeper than words — a recognition that lives in the body, in the rhythm of shared time, in the ability to sit with another person and not feel the need to fill the space.

## On Making Things

I have spent a lot of time thinking about why we make things. Not things of utility — I understand why we make chairs and roads and sandwiches — but things of no practical purpose. Paintings, poems, songs, stories. Things that do not feed us or shelter us or protect us from the rain. Things that serve no measurable function. And yet we have been making these things for as long as we have been human. The oldest cave paintings are tens of thousands of years old. Before there were cities, before there were nations, before there were books, there were handprints on cave walls. Someone stood in the dark and pressed their palm to stone and left a mark.

Why?

I think the answer might be the simplest one: because making things is how we prove we were here. It is how we say to the void, "I existed. I saw something. It mattered to me." The handprint on the cave wall is not decoration. It is testimony. It is the oldest form of the sentence we are all trying to write: I am real.

And this impulse — to make, to leave marks, to shape raw material into meaning — is not reserved for the people we call artists. Every person who bakes bread with care is making something. Every parent who tucks a child into bed and invents a story on the spot is making something. Every person who arranges flowers on a table or hums a tune while doing the dishes or writes a note on the back of a receipt and pins it to the refrigerator — these are all acts of creation. Small acts, maybe. Invisible acts, maybe. But acts nonetheless.

The trouble is that we have decided, somewhere along the way, that only certain kinds of making count. That art must be exhibited and music must be recorded and writing must be published. That the only valid creations are the ones that reach an audience. But I think this is wrong, or at least incomplete. The most important thing anyone ever makes is a moment of attention. The act of paying attention — truly paying attention, not the performative kind but the real kind, the kind that costs you something — is the foundation of every creative act and every meaningful relationship.

To pay attention is to say, "This matters." To pay attention to another person is to say, "You matter." And in a world that is constantly screaming for our attention — feeds and notifications and algorithms designed to keep us scrolling — the simple act of choosing what to attend to becomes, almost, a revolutionary act.

## The Weight of Ordinary Days

There is a kind of grief that has no name. It is not the grief of loss — we have language for that. It is not the grief of disappointment or heartbreak or failure, though it may contain elements of all three. It is the grief of ordinary time passing. The grief of watching the leaves change and realizing that another year has moved through you like water through a sieve. The grief of sitting in a car at a red light and suddenly being overwhelmed by the knowledge that this moment — this specific configuration of light and temperature and sound — will never happen again.

We are not equipped to hold the weight of this. The human mind is built for continuity, for the illusion of permanence, for the reassuring fiction that the world will still be here tomorrow, that the people we love will still be at the table when we come downstairs. And mostly, mostly, this is true. Mostly. But underneath the mostly, there is the always-changing, always-eroding, always-undoing reality of time. Everything is temporary. Everything. And we walk through our days as though this were not the case, because to walk through our days aware of it every second would be unbearable.

I think this is why poetry exists. And music. And art of every kind. Not to escape the unbearable, but to make it bearable — to frame it, to hold it up to the light and say, "Look. Even this. Even this is beautiful."

Rilke wrote that perhaps all the dragons in our lives are princesses who are only waiting to see us act, just once, with beauty and courage. Perhaps all the unbearable things in our lives are simply moments that have not yet been witnessed. Not fixed, not solved, but witnessed. Held up. Given voice.

There is a practice in some contemplative traditions of sitting with difficult emotions rather than running from them. Of turning toward the pain instead of away from it. Of saying, "I see you. I feel you. And I am here." This is not easy work. It requires a kind of courage that has nothing to do with fighting or conquering and everything to do with staying. Remaining. Allowing yourself to be in the room with the thing that hurts and not leaving.

I think we need more of this. Not just in the quiet rooms of therapists or meditation halls, but in the everyday business of being human. We need to learn to stay. To stay in conversations that are uncomfortable. To stay in relationships that are imperfect. To stay in the long middle of a life where nothing particularly dramatic is happening and yet everything is changing in slow, imperceptible ways.

## What Remains

I do not know what happens after we die. I suspect no one does, though many people are very confident about it. What I do know is what happens before we die, which is that we spend a relatively brief period of time being alive, and during that time we accumulate moments. Some of them are big — births and deaths and weddings and catastrophes. But most of them are small. A cup of coffee in the morning. The sound of someone you love breathing in the next room. The way the street looks after it rains. A sentence in a book that stops you cold because it says the thing you have felt but never articulated.

These small moments are not insignificant. They are, in fact, the entire substance of a life. They are the raw material of everything. And yet we move through them mostly unseeing, mostly unfeeling, mostly in a hurry to get to the next thing — the next meeting, the next meal, the next distraction.

What if we didn't? What if we let ourselves be slowed down by the weight of ordinary beauty? What if we noticed the particular blue of the sky on a Tuesday in October, not because it was more blue than any other blue, but because it was this blue, on this day, in this specific life we happen to be living?

I don't think this would solve our problems. The world would still be full of suffering and injustice and incomprehensible cruelty. We would still be afraid. We would still lose people we love. We would still fail at things that matter to us. But we might, in the margins of all that difficulty, find moments of extraordinary tenderness. We might find that the human experience is not only pain and not only pleasure, but something more complex and more beautiful than either word can contain.

We might find that the silence between us is not empty. That it is, in fact, full. Full of everything we have ever felt and never said. Full of the quiet, persistent hope that someone, somewhere, might understand.

And perhaps that is enough. Perhaps that is all we need. Not answers, but attention. Not solutions, but presence. Not the elimination of suffering, but the willingness to sit with it and say, "I am here. I am here. I am here."
